topic.title: Collecting Out-of-Date Content for an External Translation Agency
topic.shortdesc: How to have the agent gather the source files whose translations are missing or stale into a single folder, so that you can send them to an external translation agency.

body.p: Not every language needs to be translated by the agent. You may want a professional translation agency or an in-house translator to handle some languages, while still using to keep track of what has changed. The agent can handle the tracking for you: it knows which source files are out of date for a given target language, and it can collect exactly those files into a folder that you can hand over for human translation.

This is useful because the difficult part of working with an agency is not sending files, but knowing which files to send. Sending the whole publication every time means paying to retranslate content that has not changed, while selecting the changed files by hand is slow and easy to get wrong.

section.title: Collecting the Out-of-Date Files
section.p: Start a translation job as usual by selecting the publications and the target language that you want to send out. In the Instructions field, tell the agent not to translate anything and ask it instead to copy the source files that are not up to date into a folder that you name:

p.codeblock: Do not translate anything. Export the files that need translating into French into the `for-translation-fr/` folder.

section.p: The agent determines the translation status of each file in your selection and copies only the files with the missing or stale status. Files that are current are left out because their existing translation still matches the source. The images and other assets referenced by the publication are also collected, so that the translator can view the content in context and localize screenshots. If you want only the translatable files, say so in the instructions.

The files are copied into the folder that you named inside your workspace, while keeping their paths relative to the root of your project. A source file at en/topics/installation/install.dita is copied to for-translation-fr/en/topics/installation/install.dita, so the source-language folder is part of the copied path. Because the structure is preserved, the folder is a self-contained subset of your project that the translator can open, the relative references between the copied files continue to resolve, and a single folder can hold the files of several publications without their paths colliding.

section.title: Sending the Folder to the Agency
section.p: When the job finishes, select Bring into workspace on the job card to add the collected folder to your workspace, and review it.

To get the package out of , select the folder in the workspace file tree and choose Download. This gives you a ZIP archive of the folder that you can send to the agency. If you want to include a PDF of the publication, a glossary, or a README for the translator, upload those files into the folder before you download it.

Ask the agency to set the xml:lang attribute of each translated file's root element to the target language tag. Files that do not declare their language are rejected when the translations are brought back.
You can remove the folder after downloading it.

section.title: Bringing the Human Translations Back
section.p: When the agency returns the translated files, place them in the target-language folders of your project, using the same layout that the agent uses, and commit them. See Importing a Project with Existing Translations for information about how existing translations are recognized and recorded in the translation index. Once they are recorded, those files count as up to date, and the next round reports only what changed after that.

The same project can use both approaches. Languages translated by the agent and languages translated by an agency are tracked in the same translation index, so the out-of-date report is accurate for each language independently.
